title: Data Quality, Testing and Data Contracts
subtitle: Measure data quality, test data in pipelines with pandera, agree data contracts between producers and consumers, and catch and handle bad data before it does harm.
outcomes: Measure data against the six common dimensions of quality and report the results as a scorecard
Write pandera schemas and unit tests that validate data in a pipeline and quarantine the rows that fail
Write a data contract and classify schema changes as safe or breaking for the consumers who rely on it
Monitor freshness, volume and distributions with checks that respect seasonality, and use lineage to find impact and causes
Stop bad data with write-audit-publish, and run a data incident from detection to a blameless review
prerequisites: Python with pandas, as in Data Analysis with Python and pandas, and basic SQL from SQL for Data Analysis with DataGrip. Data Engineering Foundations: Batch and Streaming Pipelines helps. Install Python 3.10 or later and pip install "pandera[pandas]" pytest pyyaml duckdb. Monitoring Models in Production: Drift, Data Quality and Alerts and Site Reliability Engineering: SLOs, Error Budgets and Incidents make good next steps.
description:
Bad data rarely announces itself. A temperature typed in Fahrenheit, a clinic code that doesn't exist, a nightly load that quietly stopped: each one passes through a pipeline and ends up in a dashboard, a report or a model that someone trusts. This course teaches the practices that catch these problems early and handle them well when they slip through. You'll measure quality along the six common dimensions, write data tests as code with pandera and unit-test the rules themselves, and agree data contracts that say what producers promise and what consumers can rely on, with a checker that spots breaking changes before they ship.

The second half moves to production: freshness and volume monitors, anomaly checks that don't cry wolf every Sunday, lineage that tells you who an incident affects, and the write-audit-publish pattern and circuit breakers that keep bad batches away from the people who rely on them. Every lab works on the same clinic network's data, with problems planted at known places, so you can see exactly what each check catches and what it misses. The capstone has you build the whole layer for a pipeline and run a game day against it.

modules.title: What data quality means, and how to measure it
modules.summary: The dimensions of data quality, how to turn them into rules you can measure, and where in a pipeline quality breaks, with a scorecard built for a clinic network's visit extract.

lessons.title: The dimensions of data quality
objectives: Define the common dimensions of data quality, with examples
Explain why quality means fitness for a particular use
key_points: Data quality means fitness for an intended use: the same table can be good enough for a monthly trend chart and not good enough for calling individual patients back.
A widely used set of six dimensions, popularised by DAMA UK, is completeness, uniqueness, validity, accuracy, consistency and timeliness.

Completeness asks whether required values are present, uniqueness whether each real-world thing is recorded once, and validity whether values follow the rules for type, format, range and allowed values.
Accuracy asks whether values match reality, which the data alone can't prove: it needs a trusted reference, such as a sample checked against paper registers or another system of record.
Consistency asks whether values agree, within a row (a visit can't be recorded before it happened) or across datasets; timeliness asks whether data is available and up to date when it's needed.
A value can be valid but inaccurate, such as a plausible weight typed wrongly, so validity checks catch only part of the problem.

lessons.title: Turning dimensions into measurable rules
objectives: Write data quality rules as testable assertions
Profile a dataset and report a quality scorecard
key_points: A data quality rule is a testable assertion about the data, such as 'age_years is between 0 and 120', which each row either passes or fails.
Measure each rule as a count of failing rows and a pass rate, and compare the rate with a threshold agreed with the people who use the data, rather than expecting perfection.
Profiling, counting rows, nulls, distinct values, minimums, maximums and the most frequent values in each column, is the quick first look that suggests which rules to write.
One bad value can break several rules, such as a visit date in the future that also makes the record look as if it was written before the visit, so count failing rows as well as failed checks.
Report quality as a scorecard grouped by dimension and tracked over time, so problems are visible and improvements can be measured.

lessons.title: Where quality breaks in a pipeline
objectives: Identify where in a pipeline different quality problems arise
Explain why checks belong as close to the source as possible
key_points: At the source, people and systems enter wrong, missing or duplicated values, such as a temperature typed in Fahrenheit into a Celsius field.
In transit, files arrive late, twice or not at all, schemas change without warning, and encodings or time zones are misread.
In transformation, a join on a non-unique key multiplies rows, a filter silently drops records, and an inner join loses rows whose keys don't match.
Over time, data goes stale, reference lists drift and distributions shift, so checks that passed last month can fail without any code changing.
Problems are cheapest to fix close to where they start: shifting left means validating at ingestion and agreeing rules with the producers, not only cleaning up in the warehouse.

"""Write the clinic network's visit extract, with known data quality problems, to the data folder.

Only random.Random(11).random() is used, so every computer writes exactly the same rows.
Run:  python make_visits.py
"""
import csv
import random
from datetime import date, datetime, timedelta
from pathlib import Path

OUT = Path("data")
EXTRACT_DATE = date(2025, 3, 31)          # the day this extract was taken
rng = random.Random(11)


def between(lo, hi):
    return lo + int(rng.random() * (hi - lo + 1))


CLINICS = [("C01", "Pisac Health Post", "Calca"), ("C02", "Urubamba Clinic", "Urubamba"),
           ("C03", "Ollantaytambo Clinic", "Urubamba"), ("C04", "Calca Health Centre", "Calca"),
           ("C05", "Chinchero Health Post", "Urubamba"), ("C06", "Maras Health Post", "Urubamba"),
           ("C07", "Lamay Clinic", "Calca"), ("C08", "Yucay Health Post", "Urubamba")]
TESTS = ["negative", "negative", "negative", "positive", "not_done"]


def visit(n):
    day = date(2025, 3, 1) + timedelta(days=between(0, 29))
    recorded = datetime(day.year, day.month, day.day, 8) + timedelta(minutes=between(0, 36 * 60))
    age = between(0, 85)
    weight = round(3.5 + age * 0.9 if age < 18 else 48 + rng.random() * 40, 1)
    return {"visit_id": f"V{n:05d}", "patient_ref": f"P{between(1000, 1999)}", "clinic_id": CLINICS[between(0, 7)][0],
            "visit_date": day.isoformat(), "age_years": age, "weight_kg": weight,
            "temperature_c": round(36.1 + rng.random() * 2.8, 1), "malaria_test": TESTS[between(0, 4)],
            "recorded_at": recorded.isoformat(sep=" ")}


def main():
    OUT.mkdir(exist_ok=True)
    rows = [visit(n) for n in range(1, 401)]
    for i in (12, 57, 101, 188, 240, 333):                  # completeness: no patient reference
        rows[i]["patient_ref"] = ""
    for i, age in ((20, -1), (90, 140), (150, 230), (260, -4), (377, 199)):   # validity: impossible ages
        rows[i]["age_years"] = age
    for i, temp in ((33, 98.6), (144, 101.3), (299, 99.1)):  # validity: recorded in Fahrenheit
        rows[i]["temperature_c"] = temp
    for i in (5, 77, 210, 355):                              # validity: a clinic that doesn't exist
        rows[i]["clinic_id"] = "C99"
    for i in (64, 128, 192):                                 # validity: inconsistent spelling
        rows[i]["malaria_test"] = "Positive "
    for i in (45, 170, 315):                                 # consistency: recorded before the visit
        d = date.fromisoformat(rows[i]["visit_date"])
        rows[i]["recorded_at"] = datetime(d.year, d.month, d.day, 7) - timedelta(days=2)
    for i in range(380, 390):                                # timeliness: recorded 9 days after the visit
        d = date.fromisoformat(rows[i]["visit_date"])
        rows[i]["visit_date"] = (d - timedelta(days=9)).isoformat() if d.day > 10 else rows[i]["visit_date"]
        rows[i]["recorded_at"] = datetime(d.year, d.month, d.day, 16) + timedelta(days=0 if d.day > 10 else 9)
    for i in (395, 398):                                     # validity: a visit date after the extract date
        rows[i]["visit_date"] = "2025-04-12"
        rows[i]["recorded_at"] = "2025-03-30 09:15:00"
    rows += [dict(rows[i]) for i in (3, 99, 205, 311)]       # uniqueness: the same visit sent twice
    for r in rows:
        r["recorded_at"] = str(r["recorded_at"])
    with open(OUT / "visits.csv", "w", newline="", encoding="utf-8") as f:
        w = csv.DictWriter(f, fieldnames=list(rows[0]))
        w.writeheader()
        w.writerows(rows)
    with open(OUT / "clinics.csv", "w", newline="", encoding="utf-8") as f:
        w = csv.writer(f)
        w.writerow(["clinic_id", "clinic_name", "district"])
        w.writerows(CLINICS)
    with open(OUT / "register_check.csv", "w", newline="", encoding="utf-8") as f:   # a paper-register audit
        w = csv.writer(f)
        w.writerow(["visit_id", "weight_kg"])
        for i in range(0, 400, 20):
            weight = rows[i]["weight_kg"]
            w.writerow([rows[i]["visit_id"], round(weight + 10, 1) if i in (40, 160, 280) else weight])
    print(f"visits.csv: {len(rows)} rows; clinics.csv: {len(CLINICS)} rows; extract date {EXTRACT_DATE}")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

"""Score the visit extract against data quality rules, grouped by dimension.

Usage:  python profile.py
"""
import pandas as pd

EXTRACT_DATE = pd.Timestamp("2025-03-31")
ALLOWED_TESTS = ["negative", "positive", "not_done"]


def load():
    visits = pd.read_csv("data/visits.csv", parse_dates=["visit_date", "recorded_at"])
    clinics = pd.read_csv("data/clinics.csv")
    register = pd.read_csv("data/register_check.csv")
    return visits, clinics, register


def rules(visits, clinics):
    """Each rule is a boolean Series: True where a row passes."""
    delay = visits["recorded_at"] - visits["visit_date"]
    return {
        "completeness: patient_ref is present": visits["patient_ref"].notna(),
        "uniqueness: no repeated visit_id": ~visits["visit_id"].duplicated(keep="first"),
        "validity: age_years between 0 and 120": visits["age_years"].between(0, 120),
        # TODO: add these rules, named in the same style:
        #   validity: temperature_c between 30 and 45
        #   validity: malaria_test is an allowed value      (one of ALLOWED_TESTS)
        #   validity: clinic_id is a known clinic           (in clinics["clinic_id"])
        #   validity: visit_date not after the extract      (EXTRACT_DATE)
        #   consistency: recorded_at not before visit_date
        #   timeliness: recorded within 2 days              (use delay)
    }


def accuracy(visits, register):
    """Accuracy needs a trusted reference: compare weights with a sample checked against paper registers."""
    sample = register.merge(visits.drop_duplicates("visit_id"), on="visit_id", suffixes=("_register", ""))
    matches = (sample["weight_kg"] == sample["weight_kg_register"]).sum()
    return matches, len(sample)


def main():
    visits, clinics, register = load()
    print(f"{len(visits)} rows, {visits.shape[1]} columns")
    print("Null counts:", {c: int(n) for c, n in visits.isna().sum().items() if n})
    results = rules(visits, clinics)
    for name, passed in results.items():
        print(f"{name:<48} {int((~passed).sum()):>3} failing  {passed.mean():6.1%} pass")
    every = pd.concat(results, axis=1).all(axis=1)
    print(f"Rows passing every rule: {int(every.sum())} of {len(visits)}")
    matches, checked = accuracy(visits, register)
    print(f"accuracy: weight matches the register in {matches} of {checked} sampled visits")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

hints: Subtracting two datetime columns gives a timedelta; compare it with pd.Timedelta(days=2).
duplicated(keep="first") marks the second and later copies, so it counts extra copies.

modules.title: Testing data with pandera
modules.summary: Data validation as code: pandera schemas and checks, lazy validation and failure reports, quarantine, unit tests for the rules themselves, and how Great Expectations, Soda and dbt tests compare.

lessons.title: Schemas and checks in pandera
objectives: Write a pandera DataFrameSchema with column types and checks
Choose between object-based and class-based schemas
key_points: pandera validates dataframes against a schema written in Python; install it with pip install "pandera[pandas]", and current versions import the pandas API with import pandera.pandas as pa.

A DataFrameSchema maps column names to Column objects, each with a data type, checks, and options such as nullable, unique and required; coerce=True converts types, such as text to datetimes, before checking.
Built-in checks include Check.in_range, Check.isin, Check.str_matches and comparisons such as Check.le; a custom check is a function returning a boolean or a boolean Series.
Checks given to the schema itself see the whole DataFrame, which suits rules across columns, such as recorded_at not being before visit_date; strict=True rejects columns the schema doesn't know.
The class-based DataFrameModel declares the same rules as typed attributes with Field(...), and the @pa.check_types decorator validates a function's DataFrame arguments and result when it's called.
A check created with raise_warning=True issues a warning instead of failing, for rules worth watching but not worth stopping a pipeline for.

lessons.title: Validating in a pipeline: failures, quarantine and tests
objectives: Collect and report every failure with lazy validation
Quarantine failing rows, and unit-test the rules themselves
key_points: By default, validation stops at the first failure with a SchemaError; validate(df, lazy=True) runs every check and raises SchemaErrors, whose failure_cases table lists each failing value, column, check and row index.
Grouping failure_cases by check reports what failed and how often, and the row index separates the valid rows from the rows to quarantine, with their reasons.
Quarantine keeps good rows flowing while bad ones wait, with their reasons, to be fixed and replayed; use it only where partial data is acceptable, and reject the whole batch where it isn't.
Data rules are code, so unit-test them: give each rule a row that passes and a row that breaks it, and run the tests with pytest whenever the schema changes.
Validate at the boundaries: when data enters the pipeline, after transformations that could break it, and before it's published to the people and systems that rely on it.

lessons.title: Other tools: Great Expectations, Soda and dbt tests
objectives: Compare pandera with other data testing tools
Choose a tool for where the data lives
key_points: Great Expectations describes rules as expectations, such as expect_column_values_to_be_between, grouped into suites and run against batches of data, with results published as human-readable Data Docs.
Soda writes checks in a YAML-based language, SodaCL, and runs them as SQL in the warehouse, which suits data that never leaves the database.

dbt has generic data tests (unique, not_null, accepted_values and relationships) declared in YAML next to the models they test, plus singular tests written as SQL queries that return the failing rows.
pandera suits Python pipelines and dataframes in memory, and warehouse tools suit SQL pipelines; whichever you choose, keep the rules in version control and run them automatically on every load.
Tests of code and tests of data catch different problems: correct code can still receive bad data, so pipelines need both.

"""The rules a visit row must follow, as a pandera schema."""
import pandas as pd
import pandera.pandas as pa

ALLOWED_TESTS = ["negative", "positive", "not_done"]


def visit_schema(clinic_ids, extract_date):
    return pa.DataFrameSchema(
        columns={
            "visit_id": pa.Column(str, pa.Check.str_matches(r"^V\d{5}$"), unique=True,
                                  report_duplicates="exclude_first"),
            "patient_ref": pa.Column(str, pa.Check.str_matches(r"^P\d{4}$"), nullable=False),
            "clinic_id": pa.Column(str),          # TODO: only the clinics in clinic_ids
            "visit_date": pa.Column(pa.DateTime, pa.Check.le(extract_date)),
            "age_years": pa.Column(int, pa.Check.in_range(0, 120)),
            "weight_kg": pa.Column(float, pa.Check.in_range(0.5, 300)),
            "temperature_c": pa.Column(float),    # TODO: between 30 and 45 degrees Celsius
            "malaria_test": pa.Column(str),       # TODO: one of ALLOWED_TESTS
            "recorded_at": pa.Column(pa.DateTime),
        },
        checks=[
            # TODO: a dataframe-wide check, named recorded_after_visit with the error message
            # "recorded_at is before visit_date", that fails rows where recorded_at < visit_date
            pa.Check(lambda df: df["recorded_at"] - df["visit_date"] <= pd.Timedelta(days=2),
                     name="recorded_within_2_days", raise_warning=True),
        ],
        strict=True,     # no columns the contract doesn't know about
        coerce=True,     # convert types where possible, such as text dates to datetimes
    )

"""Validate the visit extract with pandera, report every failure, and quarantine the rows that fail.

Usage:  python validate_visits.py
"""
import warnings
from pathlib import Path

import pandas as pd
import pandera.pandas as pa

from visit_schema import visit_schema

EXTRACT_DATE = pd.Timestamp("2025-03-31")


def split(visits, schema):
    """Return (valid rows, rejected rows with their reasons, a summary of failures by column and check)."""
    try:
        schema.validate(visits, lazy=True)          # lazy: collect every failure instead of stopping at one
        return visits, visits.iloc[0:0], None
    except pa.errors.SchemaErrors as err:
        cases = err.failure_cases.dropna(subset=["index"])
        # A dataframe-wide check reports every column of a failing row; label those failures "row".
        target = cases["column"].where(cases["schema_context"] == "Column", "row")
        cases = cases.assign(reason=target + ": " + cases["check"].astype(str))
        reasons = cases.groupby("index")["reason"].apply(lambda r: "; ".join(sorted(set(r))))
        bad = visits.index.isin(reasons.index)
        rejected = visits[bad].assign(reasons=reasons)
        summary = cases.groupby("reason")["index"].nunique()
        return visits[~bad], rejected, summary


def main():
    visits = pd.read_csv("data/visits.csv", dtype={"patient_ref": "string"})
    clinic_ids = pd.read_csv("data/clinics.csv")["clinic_id"].tolist()
    schema = visit_schema(clinic_ids, EXTRACT_DATE)
    with warnings.catch_warnings(record=True) as caught:
        warnings.simplefilter("always")
        valid, rejected, summary = split(visits, schema)
    for w in caught:
        if "recorded_within_2_days" in str(w.message):
            print("Warning: some visits were recorded more than 2 days late")
    if summary is not None:
        print("Rows failing each check:")
        for reason, count in summary.items():
            print(f"  {reason}: {count}")
    Path("clean").mkdir(exist_ok=True)
    Path("quarantine").mkdir(exist_ok=True)
    valid.to_csv("clean/visits_valid.csv", index=False)
    rejected.to_csv("quarantine/visits_rejected.csv", index=False)
    print(f"valid rows: {len(valid)}; quarantined rows: {len(rejected)}")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

"""Unit tests for the visit schema: each rule gets a row that breaks it. Run with:  pytest -q"""
import pandas as pd
import pandera.pandas as pa
import pytest

from visit_schema import visit_schema

GOOD = {"visit_id": "V00001", "patient_ref": "P1507", "clinic_id": "C05", "visit_date": "2025-03-14",
        "age_years": 79, "weight_kg": 66.6, "temperature_c": 36.6, "malaria_test": "negative",
        "recorded_at": "2025-03-15 04:09:00"}
SCHEMA = visit_schema(["C01", "C05"], pd.Timestamp("2025-03-31"))
FAILS = (pa.errors.SchemaError, pa.errors.SchemaErrors)   # some failures are collected into SchemaErrors


def frame(*rows):
    return pd.DataFrame([{**GOOD, **changes} for changes in rows])


def test_a_good_row_passes():
    SCHEMA.validate(frame({}))


@pytest.mark.parametrize("changes", [
    {"age_years": -1},                                   # impossible age
    {"temperature_c": 98.6},                             # Fahrenheit in a Celsius column
    {"malaria_test": "Positive "},                       # not one of the allowed values
    {"clinic_id": "C99"},                                # unknown clinic
    {"patient_ref": None},                               # missing patient reference
    {"visit_date": "2025-04-12", "recorded_at": "2025-04-12 09:00:00"},   # after the extract date
    {"recorded_at": "2025-03-12 07:00:00"},              # recorded before the visit
], ids=["age", "fahrenheit", "test-value", "clinic", "patient-ref", "future-date", "recorded-early"])
def test_a_broken_rule_fails(changes):
    with pytest.raises(FAILS):
        SCHEMA.validate(frame(changes))


def test_a_repeated_visit_id_fails():
    with pytest.raises(FAILS):
        SCHEMA.validate(frame({}, {}))


def test_an_unexpected_column_fails():
    with pytest.raises(FAILS):
        SCHEMA.validate(frame({}).assign(notes="free text"))

modules.title: Schema evolution and data contracts
modules.summary: How schemas change without breaking consumers, what a data contract between producers and consumers contains, and how to enforce contracts in CI and at run time, with a checker that classifies changes as safe or breaking.

lessons.title: Schema evolution: safe and breaking changes
objectives: Classify schema changes as safe or breaking for consumers
Plan a breaking change with expand and contract
key_points: A change is safe for existing consumers when every dataset valid under the new schema is also valid under the old one, so code built on the old schema keeps working.

Adding a column, making a column required and narrowing a range or a list of allowed values are usually safe; removing or renaming a column, changing its type, allowing nulls and adding allowed values are breaking.
Semantic changes break consumers without changing the schema: a temperature switched from Celsius to Fahrenheit, or revenue switched from gross to net, passes every type check.
Expand and contract makes a breaking change safely: add the new column beside the old one, fill both, move consumers over, then remove the old column in a new major version after a notice period.
Apache Iceberg tracks columns by ID, so renaming or reordering columns doesn't corrupt old data; plain CSV and Parquet files rely on column names or positions, so treat a rename there as breaking.

lessons.title: What a data contract contains
objectives: Describe the parts of a data contract
Explain the responsibilities of producers and consumers
key_points: A data contract is an agreement, kept as a versioned file, between the team that produces a dataset and the teams that consume it, about what the data looks like, what it means and how it's delivered.
It names the dataset and its owner, gives the schema (fields, types, required fields, allowed values and ranges), defines each field's meaning and units, and lists quality rules.
It also sets service levels, such as how fresh the data will be and how many rows a normal day brings, and the change process: how much notice a breaking change gets and how versions are numbered.
Semantic versioning suits contracts: a breaking change needs a new major version, a safe addition a new minor version, and a wording fix a patch.

Open standards such as the Open Data Contract Standard (ODCS) describe contracts in YAML, and open-source tools such as the Data Contract CLI can lint a contract, test data against it and report breaking changes.
The producer owns meeting the contract and announcing changes; consumers own relying only on what the contract promises, not on accidents of today's data.

lessons.title: Enforcing contracts in CI and at run time
objectives: Enforce a contract before changes merge and while data flows
Decide what happens when a batch violates its contract
key_points: In CI, a check compares the proposed contract or schema with the published one and fails the build if a change is breaking without a new major version, so the problem is found in review, not in production.
At run time, each batch is validated against the contract as it's produced or ingested; a violation blocks or quarantines the batch and alerts the producer, not just the consumers.
Generating validation code, such as a pandera schema, from the contract file keeps the rules in one place, so the documentation and the checks can't drift apart.
Consumer-driven tests let each consumer add checks for the guarantees it actually relies on, which tells producers exactly who a change would affect.
A contract works only if both sides own it: it needs a named owner, a channel for questions, and a review of breaking changes with the consumers before they ship.

modules.title: Monitoring: freshness, volume, anomalies and lineage
modules.summary: Watching data in production: freshness and volume checks, anomaly detection that respects seasonality and resists outliers, and lineage that shows what a problem affects and where it came from.

lessons.title: Freshness and volume checks
objectives: Define freshness and volume checks with thresholds
Explain why monitoring complements rule-based tests
key_points: Rule-based tests check what's in a batch; monitoring watches data over time, catching problems no rule describes, such as a table that has silently stopped updating.
A freshness check compares the time of the newest data, or of the last successful load, with now, and alerts when the gap passes the service level, such as 26 hours for a daily load.
Volume checks compare row counts with what's expected: a sudden drop often means a source or a load partly failed, and a sudden jump often means duplicates.
Schema checks watch for columns added, removed or retyped, and distribution checks watch metrics such as null rates, distinct counts and averages of key columns.
Data observability is the name for these checks together, usually with lineage, so data teams find problems before the people using the data do.

lessons.title: Anomaly detection without the false alarms
objectives: Detect anomalies in data metrics with z-scores and robust statistics
Account for seasonality and avoid alert fatigue
key_points: A z-score measures how many standard deviations a value is from the mean of recent history; flagging |z| above a threshold such as 3 is simple, but spikes and patterns in the history inflate the standard deviation and hide real problems.
Robust statistics resist outliers: the modified z-score, 0.6745 x (value - median) / MAD, uses the median and the median absolute deviation, and a common rule of thumb flags scores above 3.5.
Seasonality causes false alarms: a clinic network that loads fewer rows every Sunday trips a naive check each week, so compare each day with the same weekday in previous weeks.

Every alert should lead to an action: too many false alarms teach people to ignore alerts (alert fatigue), so tune thresholds on history, route alerts to the dataset's owner and review them regularly.
Check the direction that matters: a rising null rate is a problem while a falling one usually isn't, so a one-sided test raises fewer false alarms.

lessons.title: Lineage: impact and root cause
objectives: Use lineage to find what a data problem affects
Trace a problem upstream to its likely cause
key_points: Lineage records how data flows: which jobs read which datasets and write which others, at table level or, more precisely, at column level.
Downstream lineage answers impact questions: when a table is wrong, which reports, dashboards and models use it, and which owners must be told.
Upstream lineage answers root-cause questions: which sources and jobs fed a broken dashboard, and so where to look first.

OpenLineage is an open standard for collecting lineage: jobs emit run events, such as START, COMPLETE and FAIL, naming their input and output datasets; integrations exist for Airflow, Spark and dbt, and Marquez is its reference implementation.
Lineage is a graph, so a breadth-first search along its edges, forwards for impact or backwards for causes, lists every affected or contributing asset.

"""Write 60 days of load statistics for the visits table to data/load_stats.csv.

Each row is one nightly load: when it finished, how many rows it loaded, and the share of rows with no
patient reference. Only random.Random(5).random() is used, so the file is the same on every computer.
Run:  python make_load_stats.py
"""
import csv
import random
from datetime import date, datetime, timedelta
from pathlib import Path

rng = random.Random(5)


def main():
    Path("data").mkdir(exist_ok=True)
    rows = []
    for n in range(60):
        day = date(2025, 1, 1) + timedelta(days=n)
        sunday = day.weekday() == 6
        loaded = (30 if sunday else 120) + int(rng.random() * 11) - 5
        null_rate = round(0.005 + rng.random() * 0.01, 4)
        if day == date(2025, 2, 11):
            loaded = 52                     # a clinic's upload failed: about half the rows are missing
        if day == date(2025, 2, 20):
            null_rate = 0.095               # a form change stopped patient references being saved
        finished = datetime(day.year, day.month, day.day, 2) + timedelta(days=1, minutes=int(rng.random() * 40))
        rows.append([day.isoformat(), "visits", loaded, null_rate, finished.isoformat(sep=" ")])
    with open("data/load_stats.csv", "w", newline="", encoding="utf-8") as f:
        w = csv.writer(f)
        w.writerow(["load_date", "table_name", "rows_loaded", "null_rate_patient_ref", "finished_at"])
        w.writerows(rows)
    print(f"load_stats.csv: {len(rows)} loads, {rows[0][0]} to {rows[-1][0]}")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

"""Freshness, volume and anomaly checks on the visits table's load statistics.

Usage:  python monitor.py
"""
import pandas as pd

NOW = pd.Timestamp("2025-03-03 09:00")     # when the monitor runs
FRESHNESS_SLA_HOURS = 26


def freshness(stats):
    age = (NOW - stats["finished_at"].max()) / pd.Timedelta(hours=1)
    status = "OK" if age <= FRESHNESS_SLA_HOURS else "STALE"
    print(f"freshness: last load finished {age:.1f} hours ago (SLA {FRESHNESS_SLA_HOURS} h): {status}")


def volume_zscore(stats, window=14, threshold=3.0):
    """Naive check: compare each day with the mean and standard deviation of the previous 14 days."""
    rows = stats["rows_loaded"]
    mean = rows.shift(1).rolling(window).mean()
    std = rows.shift(1).rolling(window).std()
    z = (rows - mean) / std
    return stats.loc[z.abs() > threshold, "load_date"].dt.strftime("%Y-%m-%d (%a)").tolist()


def volume_seasonal(stats, weeks=4, tolerance=0.3):
    """Compare each day with the median of the same weekday over the previous four weeks."""

    # work out the relative change from that median, and return the dates where its size is above tolerance,
    # formatted like the other checks. Days without four weeks of history can't be judged.
    return []


def null_rate_robust(stats, window=28, threshold=3.5):
    """Modified z-score: distance from the median in units of the median absolute deviation (MAD)."""

    # deviation (MAD: the median of |x - median|); score = 0.6745 * (rate - median) / MAD; return the dates
    # whose score is above threshold. Only rises matter here: more missing references, not fewer.

def main():
    stats = pd.read_csv("data/load_stats.csv", parse_dates=["load_date", "finished_at"])
    freshness(stats)
    print("volume, naive z-score above 3:", volume_zscore(stats, threshold=3.0))
    print("volume, naive z-score above 2:", volume_zscore(stats, threshold=2.0))
    print("volume, same weekday median:", volume_seasonal(stats))
    print("null rate, modified z-score:", null_rate_robust(stats))


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

"""Use table-level lineage to find what a data problem affects (downstream) and where it may come from (upstream).

Usage:  python impact.py downstream staging.visits_clean
        python impact.py upstream "dashboard: malaria cases by district"
"""
import json
import sys
from collections import deque


def walk(start, edges, direction):
    """Breadth-first search over the lineage graph, in either direction."""
    nexts = {}
    for source, target in edges:
        a, b = (source, target) if direction == "downstream" else (target, source)
        nexts.setdefault(a, []).append(b)
    seen, queue, order = {start}, deque([start]), []
    while queue:
        for node in sorted(nexts.get(queue.popleft(), [])):
            if node not in seen:
                seen.add(node)
                order.append(node)
                queue.append(node)
    return order


def main():
    direction, start = sys.argv[1], sys.argv[2]
    lineage = json.load(open("lineage.json", encoding="utf-8"))
    found = walk(start, lineage["edges"], direction)
    print(f"{direction} of {start}: {len(found)} assets")
    for node in found:
        owner = lineage["owners"].get(node)
        print(f"  {node}" + (f"  (tell: {owner})" if owner else ""))


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

rolling(window).apply(lambda x: (abs(x - x.median())).median(), raw=False) gives the MAD.
Flag only score > threshold, not the absolute value: a falling null rate isn't a problem.

modules.title: Handling data incidents
modules.summary: When bad data gets through: severity, containment, communication, backfills and blameless reviews, and the patterns, write-audit-publish and circuit breakers, that keep bad data away from the people who rely on it.

lessons.title: The data incident lifecycle
objectives: Run a data incident from detection to resolution
Communicate with the people affected
key_points: A data incident is any event in which data that people or systems rely on is wrong, late or missing, and it deserves the same discipline as a service outage.
Triage sets the severity by impact: who uses the data, for which decisions, and how much of it is affected, which lineage helps answer quickly.
Contain first: pause the pipeline or the affected downstream jobs, mark dashboards as under investigation, and stop bad data spreading before working on the cause.
Communicate early and regularly through the channel the contract names: what's affected, what people should do in the meantime, and when the next update will come.
Resolve by fixing the cause, correcting the data and backfilling the affected partitions with idempotent re-runs, then confirm the numbers are right before closing the incident.

lessons.title: Prevention patterns and blameless reviews
objectives: Use write-audit-publish and circuit breakers to stop bad data
Write a blameless incident review with actions
key_points: Write-audit-publish (WAP) writes each batch to a staging area, runs the audits there, and publishes it, usually in a single transaction or an atomic swap, only if every audit passes.
A circuit breaker stops downstream jobs, such as dashboard refreshes and model training, when upstream checks fail, so a bad batch doesn't flow on automatically.
Table formats such as Apache Iceberg and Delta Lake keep snapshots, so a table can be rolled back to before a bad load, and Iceberg branches support write-audit-publish directly.
A runbook for each important dataset lists its checks, owners and consumers, and the steps to pause, fix and backfill it, so whoever is on call can act quickly.
A blameless review records the timeline, impact, root cause and actions with owners, and asks what the system allowed rather than who made a mistake, so people report problems early.
Every incident should leave a new or better check behind, so the same failure is caught automatically next time.

"""Write three daily visit batches to the batches folder: a clean one for 10 March, a broken one for
11 March, and the corrected file the clinic records team sends for 11 March after the incident.

Only random.Random(3).random() is used, so the files are the same on every computer.
Run:  python make_batches.py
"""
import csv
import random
from pathlib import Path

rng = random.Random(3)
FIELDS = ["visit_id", "patient_ref", "clinic_id", "visit_date", "age_years", "weight_kg", "temperature_c",
          "malaria_test", "recorded_at"]


def between(lo, hi):
    return lo + int(rng.random() * (hi - lo + 1))


def day_rows(day, first_id, count):
    rows = []
    for n in range(count):
        age = between(1, 80)
        rows.append([f"V{first_id + n:05d}", f"P{between(1000, 1999)}", f"C0{between(1, 8)}", day, age,
                     round(9 + age * 0.8 if age < 18 else 50 + rng.random() * 35, 1),
                     round(36.2 + rng.random() * 2.5, 1), ["negative", "positive", "not_done"][between(0, 2)],
                     f"{day} {between(8, 17):02d}:{between(0, 59):02d}:00"])
    return rows


def write(name, rows):
    with open(Path("batches") / name, "w", newline="", encoding="utf-8") as f:
        w = csv.writer(f)
        w.writerow(FIELDS)
        w.writerows(rows)
    print(f"{name}: {len(rows)} rows")


def main():
    Path("batches").mkdir(exist_ok=True)
    write("visits_2025-03-10.csv", day_rows("2025-03-10", 20001, 12))
    good = day_rows("2025-03-11", 20013, 14)
    broken = [list(r) for r in good] + [list(good[3])]   # one visit sent twice
    broken[5][2] = "C99"                                 # an unknown clinic
    broken[8][1] = ""                                    # a missing patient reference
    write("visits_2025-03-11.csv", broken)
    write("visits_2025-03-11_v2.csv", good)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

"""Write-audit-publish for daily visit batches: load a batch into staging, audit it there, and publish it to
the table people query only if every audit passes. Downstream refreshes run only after a publish.

Usage:  python wap.py batches/visits_2025-03-10.csv
        python wap.py --report
"""
import sys
from pathlib import Path

import duckdb

DB = "clinic.duckdb"
AUDITS = {   # each query counts problem rows in staging; 0 means the audit passes
    "has rows": "SELECT CASE WHEN count(*) = 0 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END FROM staging",
    "one visit date": "SELECT count(DISTINCT visit_date) - 1 FROM staging",
    "no repeated visit_id": "SELECT count(*) - count(DISTINCT visit_id) FROM staging",
    "patient_ref present": "SELECT count(*) FROM staging WHERE patient_ref IS NULL",
    "known clinic": "SELECT count(*) FROM staging WHERE clinic_id NOT IN (SELECT clinic_id FROM clinics)",
    "temperature 30 to 45": "SELECT count(*) FROM staging WHERE temperature_c NOT BETWEEN 30 AND 45",
}
COLUMNS = ("visit_id VARCHAR, patient_ref VARCHAR, clinic_id VARCHAR, visit_date DATE, age_years INTEGER, "
           "weight_kg DOUBLE, temperature_c DOUBLE, malaria_test VARCHAR, recorded_at TIMESTAMP")


def setup(con):
    con.execute("CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS clinics AS SELECT * FROM read_csv('data/clinics.csv', header = true)")
    con.execute(f"CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS visits ({COLUMNS})")
    con.execute(f"CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS quarantine (source_file VARCHAR, failed_audits VARCHAR, {COLUMNS})")
    con.execute("CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS audit_log (source_file VARCHAR, audit VARCHAR, problem_rows INTEGER, "
                "checked_at TIMESTAMP)")


def run(con, path):
    name = Path(path).name
    # WRITE: the batch goes to staging, never straight into the published table
    con.execute(f"CREATE OR REPLACE TABLE staging ({COLUMNS})")
    con.execute("INSERT INTO staging SELECT * FROM read_csv(?, header = true, all_varchar = true)", [str(path)])
    # AUDIT: every check runs against staging, and every result is logged
    results = {audit: con.execute(sql).fetchone()[0] for audit, sql in AUDITS.items()}
    for audit, problems in results.items():
        con.execute("INSERT INTO audit_log VALUES (?, ?, ?, current_timestamp)", [name, audit, problems])
    failed = {audit: n for audit, n in results.items() if n}
    staged = con.execute("SELECT count(*) FROM staging").fetchone()[0]
    # TODO: the gate. If any audit failed, copy the staged rows into quarantine with the file name and a
    # summary such as "known clinic (1), patient_ref present (1)", print a line starting
    # f"{name}: BLOCKED, failed audits: ..." and return False, so nothing is published.
    # PUBLISH: replace this date's rows in one transaction, so readers see all of the batch or none of it
    day = con.execute("SELECT min(visit_date) FROM staging").fetchone()[0]
    con.execute("BEGIN TRANSACTION")
    replaced = con.execute("DELETE FROM visits WHERE visit_date = ?", [day]).fetchone()[0]
    con.execute("INSERT INTO visits SELECT * FROM staging")
    con.execute("COMMIT")
    print(f"{name}: published {staged} rows for {day} ({replaced} replaced)")
    return True


def refresh_downstream(con):
    rows = con.execute("SELECT count(*) FROM visits").fetchone()[0]
    print(f"downstream: dashboard extract rebuilt from {rows} published rows")


def report(con):
    for day, rows in con.execute("SELECT visit_date, count(*) FROM visits GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY 1").fetchall():
        print(f"published {day}: {rows} rows")
    for source, failed, rows in con.execute("SELECT source_file, any_value(failed_audits), count(*) "
                                            "FROM quarantine GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY 1").fetchall():
        print(f"quarantined {source}: {rows} rows ({failed})")


def main():
    if len(sys.argv) != 2:
        sys.exit(__doc__)
    con = duckdb.connect(DB)
    setup(con)
    if sys.argv[1] == "--report":
        report(con)
    elif run(con, sys.argv[1]):
        refresh_downstream(con)          # the circuit breaker: nothing downstream runs after a blocked batch
    else:
        print("downstream: refresh skipped, an incident needs triage")
    con.close()


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

# Data incident report

Keep it blameless: describe what the system and the process allowed, not who made a mistake.

## Summary
What happened, in two or three sentences.

## Impact
Which tables, dashboards, reports and models were affected, for how long, and who relies on them.

## Timeline
When the bad data arrived, when it was detected and how, when consumers were told, when it was contained,
fixed and backfilled. Use times, not just dates.

## Detection
Which check caught it, or who noticed. Could a check have caught it sooner?

## Root cause
Why the bad data was produced, and why it got as far as it did. Ask "why?" until you reach something you can change.

## Resolution
What was done to contain it, correct it and backfill, and how you confirmed the data was right again.

## What went well, and what didn't

## Actions
Each with an owner and a date: new or stricter checks, contract changes, alerts, runbook updates.

hints: INSERT INTO quarantine SELECT ?, ?, * FROM staging copies the staged rows with the file name and the summary in front.
Return before the BEGIN TRANSACTION, so a blocked batch never touches the published table.
Publishing deletes the date's rows and inserts the new ones in one transaction, which is why a repeat is safe.

study_plan.focus: Learn the dimensions of data quality, and score the clinic extract in the module 1 lab.
Write pandera schemas and unit tests, and validate and quarantine the visits.
Study schema evolution and data contracts, and catch a breaking change with the contract checker.
Monitor freshness, volume and anomalies, and trace impact with lineage.
Handle data incidents, and stop a bad batch with write-audit-publish.
Build and submit the capstone quality layer, then review with the mock exam and the flashcards.

project.title: Build a quality and contract layer for a pipeline
project.brief: Take a pipeline, either the clinic visits from this course extended with a second table (such as laboratory results) or a dataset of your own with at least two tables, and give it the protection a team would rely on. Write a data contract for each published dataset, enforce it with pandera in CI and at run time, monitor freshness, volume and at least one distribution metric with checks that respect seasonality, record its lineage, and publish every batch through write-audit-publish with a circuit breaker. Then run a game day: inject at least three different problems, such as a breaking schema change, a partial load and a silent unit change, show which checks catch each one (and admit which don't), and write a blameless review of one of them.
deliverables: Data contracts in YAML with owners, schemas, meanings and units, quality rules, service levels and a change policy, under version control
pandera schemas built from or matching the contracts, pytest unit tests for every rule, and a CI step that fails on a breaking contract change without a new major version
A monitoring script for freshness, volume and a distribution metric with seasonal or robust thresholds, and its output over at least 30 days of history
A lineage graph of the pipeline and an impact report for one failing table
A write-audit-publish loader with quarantine and a circuit breaker, and the output of a run that blocks a bad batch and then publishes the corrected one
A game-day log: each injected problem, the check that caught it or why none did, and the fix
A blameless incident review for one problem, with actions, owners and dates

rubric.name: Contracts and versioning
rubric.description: Contracts are complete and specific, including units and service levels; versions follow the change policy; breaking changes are caught in CI.

rubric.name: Tests and validation
rubric.description: Every rule has passing and failing unit tests; run-time validation reports every failure and quarantines or blocks as the contract says.

rubric.name: Monitoring
rubric.description: Freshness, volume and distribution checks run on real history, with thresholds chosen to avoid false alarms and justified.

rubric.name: Prevention
rubric.description: Write-audit-publish publishes atomically and idempotently; the circuit breaker stops downstream work after a failed audit.

rubric.name: Game day and lineage
rubric.description: At least three different problems injected and traced; gaps in coverage are admitted and followed up; impact is worked out from lineage.

rubric.name: Incident review
rubric.description: Blameless, with a clear timeline, impact, root cause and actions that would prevent or catch the problem next time.

project.submit: Paste your contracts, a link to your repository (or your code), the CI output for a breaking change, the monitor and loader outputs, your game-day log and your incident review.
